newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: More Czech crown losses seen as market mood sours.
newsitem.headline: More Czech crown losses seen as market mood sours.

text.p: Profit-taking and changing market sentiment pulled the Czech crown lower on Thursday, and dealers said they expected further weakness since there were few fundamentals to support the unit.

Once one of Europe's most stable currencies, confidence in the crown has been shaken badly in the past two weeks following central bank comments that the crown was overvalued and interest rate cuts may be imminent.
In late afternoon trading, the crown was at 28.873 against the dollar and 17.090 to the mark, implying +2.74 percent against the basket midpoint, down from an opening at +3.53 percent.

"The fall is part profit-taking and part change in market sentiment," said Breta Tichanek of ING Bank here. "We are really seeing an outflow of investment from the crown at this moment, but I don't think it will last for more than a couple of weeks."
At midday, the central bank followed the early downtrend with its daily fixing, putting the crown/dollar at 28.784 and crown/mark at 17.040, or +3.03 against the basket.
Crown woes also follow recent media reports that German banks see the crown moving lower and are advising clients to stay away from Czech bonds.
"The market has been very nervous, and I think the German media reports were the last straw for some investors. They have decided to take their profits now and run," said a London-based trader.

Before this recent attack, the crown had strengthened since the beginning of the year by about three percent against the basket on demand from a wave of over 35 billion crowns ($1.2 billion) worth of crown-denominated Eurobonds.
At the crown's peak earlier this month, before talk of possible central bank intervention on the market, it was up at +5.5 percent over parity.

Many investors had boosted the crown, taking advantage of a high interest rate differential with western Europe, but the central bank comments coupled with softer interbank market rates have taken away much of the crown's lustre.
Prague Interbank Offered Rates (PRIBOR) on Thursday traded between 11.5-12.5 percent, down about 60-70 basis points from the year's start.

"I think the market is on a calm wave...we expect further tests for the Czech crown weakening. We see also movement on the money market and money market derivatives," said Petr Korous of Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.
Tichanek saw little chance the currency would come close to returning to its highs earlier this month, noting the crown was having trouble finding strong support at current levels.
Longer-term, some analysts expected a growing trade deficit to keep the crown down this year.
The Czech Statistical Bureau predicts a 1997 deficit between 211 and 219 billion crowns, up from last year's record 106.3-billion crown shortfall.
